events.c: An earlier landing damaged the rear fuselage and the wall that holds cabin pressure.
An incorrect repair left part of the pressure wall's joint weakened. Inspectors missed the error.
The flight taxied out with the first officer training for command and the captain in the right seat.
The aircraft began its takeoff run.
The aircraft took off from Haneda for Osaka.
Controllers approved a direct route to Seaperch as the aircraft climbed.
A loud sound accompanied unusual movement. The repaired pressure wall likely failed, damaging the rear fuselage and tail.
The aircraft abruptly accelerated forward.
The autopilot switched off.
The captain requested a descent and a return to Haneda.
The crew acknowledged instructions to turn right, but the aircraft did not follow the intended return route.
The aircraft began repeatedly climbing, descending, and swaying. The controls could not stop this after hydraulic control failed.
Rescue coordinators began gathering information about the aircraft's emergency.
The captain told controllers the aircraft could not be controlled.
Controllers offered Nagoya as a landing option. The crew again requested Haneda.
The flight engineer urged oxygen mask use. It is unclear whether the flight crew wore them.
The main landing gear extended.
The sun set at the crash site at about 6:40 p.m.
Engine power fell substantially, and the aircraft descended faster.
The crew again requested directions to Haneda. Controllers gave an eastward heading and a runway.
Mountains increasingly disrupted radar tracking of the aircraft.
Airspeed reached its recorded minimum of 108 knots, with the wing at a steep angle to the airflow.
Movable panels along the wings' front edges began extending, except those on the outer sections.
The panels along the wings' front edges finished extending, except those on the outer sections.
The crew asked their position. Controllers described where the aircraft was relative to Haneda and Kumagaya.
Controllers told the crew that both Haneda and Yokota were available for landing.
The flaps began retracting as the aircraft tilted farther to the right.
The aircraft's nose dropped into a steep descent, and engine power increased.
The aircraft crashed on the ridge at about 6:56 p.m. The exact time it stopped is unknown.
The aircraft pointed about 36 degrees nose down and tilted about 70 degrees to the right.
A warning sounded about nearby ground. Engine power increased, and the descent briefly stopped.
The right wing struck trees near a ridge. The outer right engine likely broke away.
The aircraft struck another ridge, then continued toward the main crash ridge.
The final flight recorder reading shows the nose steeply down and the aircraft rolled beyond vertical.
Rescue coordinators received notice that the aircraft had disappeared from radar.
Two Japanese fighter jets took off to search for the aircraft.
A US military transport aircraft reported a fire, but its reported position was about three kilometers off.
Two fighter jets reported flames, but their reported position was about six kilometers off.
A Japanese rescue helicopter observed flames, but its reported position was about four kilometers off.
A US navigator later recalled orders to return despite a helicopter's offer to lower rescuers nearby.
A helicopter's attempt to guide police from the air failed, about two kilometers from the crash site.
Military searchers reported finding wreckage, but their reported position was about three kilometers from the crash site.
A police helicopter identified the crash site.
Rescuers found four survivors among the wreckage. All had been seated in the rear cabin.
All four survivors had been freed from the wreckage.
A military helicopter carried all four survivors away for medical treatment.
Investigators linked an incorrect repair to cracking, pressure wall failure, and loss of tail and hydraulic control.
Safety investigators addressed disputed issues and acknowledged gaps in earlier explanations and rescue records.
The safety board said an unidentified seabed object did not justify reopening the investigation.
Boeing reported no new repair facts; the aviation regulator supplied no additional information.

numbers.label: Landings after repair, before accident flight
Sound to final flight recorder reading
Final recorded tilt to the right

one_line: An incorrectly repaired pressure wall failed, damaging the tail and controls before a mountain crash.
status_why: Wreckage and flight recordings support the repair failure explanation; questions remain about rescue decisions and why the repair went wrong.
